results.input: Competitive AI RPG/companion/long-agent failure modes; 100–500-turn endurance patterns; recognition UX; contradiction quarantine using aviation, legal e-discovery, and wiki conflict mechanisms.

output.confidence_notes: The HORIZON paper is a 2026 arXiv preprint and should be treated as promising but not yet settled consensus; its reported trajectory counts and agreement metrics are confirmed as stated on the paper page, while generalization to a narrative RPG is an engineering extrapolation. The agent-memory UX source is an ACM publication, but detailed design recommendations here are synthesis rather than direct product requirements. FAA SMS, FRCP Rule 26, and MediaWiki history are authoritative analogies, not evidence that their procedures are legally or operationally required for a game. No vendor-specific competitor claim is used; any unverified claim about commercial AI companions, proprietary memory behavior, or rumored benchmark performance is intentionally omitted or should be labeled SPECULATIVE. Legal/e-discovery analogies are not legal advice; obtain counsel before representing the game’s data practices as compliant with any jurisdiction.
output.research_notes:
# Research Notes

## Evidence-backed failure patterns

**Long-horizon degradation changes the failure mix, not merely the success rate.** HORIZON’s 3,100+ trajectory study across four domains reports that planning failures and memory failures—especially subplanning errors and catastrophic forgetting—become dominant as the horizon increases; it argues that base-model scaling alone is insufficient and that planning, memory, and execution-time controls are needed [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.11978v1). For SynapticGM, treat 100–500 turns as a distinct reliability regime: run fixed-seed endurance campaigns at 100, 250, and 500 turns, inject corrections and delayed callbacks, and score invariant preservation separately from prose quality.

A useful competitor-pattern comparison is therefore not “which companion remembers more,” but **which system exposes a durable, inspectable state transition and recovers after an error**. A model-generated recap or RAG hit may help produce flavor, but it is not evidence of a committed world change. The ledger-first rule should remain strict: player correction > pinned canon/opening invariant > accepted `StateTx` > `SceneManifest` > supporting evidence > draft invention.

| Observed/established pattern | SynapticGM implementation mapping | Gate or test |
|---|---|---|
| Memory and planning errors compound with horizon [1] | `CampaignContract` owns invariant IDs; every accepted `StateTx` carries causal parent, actor, turn, and affected entity/version | Endurance replay: no HP, inventory, quest, roster, or relationship field may change without a valid `StateTx` |
| Tool/action hallucination and false completion are dangerous long-agent classes [1] | `IntentContract` describes requested operation; server validates preconditions and emits either committed `StateTx` or explicit rejection | Negative test: fabricated “I found the key” narration cannot create an item; absent tool receipt blocks commit |
| Memory correction must be durable and inspectable; users often have incomplete mental models of agent memory [2] | Correction UI creates a typed correction transaction, not an overwritten summary; expose “what changed / why / source / superseded version” | Correction persistence test across scene reload, compaction, and 500-turn replay; verify old claim remains auditable but non-authoritative |

## Recognition UX: make state legible before asking for trust

The HCI evidence favors explicit capability and memory communication rather than invisible persistence. A 2025 study on users’ expectations and practices with agent memory found that users often have incomplete mental models of what agents remember and how remembered information affects behavior, and identifies task-based organization and access control as design opportunities [2](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706599.3720158). Conversational grounding research likewise treats acknowledgement and repair as mechanisms for establishing common ground [3](https://www.justinecassell.com/articulab/projects/convers-ground/).

Implement a compact **recognition card** at the moment a durable fact is used: “Using ledger fact: Mira owes you 3 coins (StateTx #184, turn 72).” Provide one-tap **Correct**, **Inspect**, and **Not canon / quarantine** actions. The assistant should acknowledge the correction in plain language, then show the resulting transaction ID; it should not claim that a summary was “updated” unless the authoritative ledger actually changed. For uncertain or merely evidentiary material, label it “evidence,” “proposal,” or “draft invention,” never “remembered fact.”

Recommended mechanism mapping is: `IntroductionPermit` gates whether a new NPC/faction/item may be introduced; `HookArc` and `beatFingerprint` are continuity aids and duplicate-hook detectors, not world truth; `SceneManifest` is a renderable projection of accepted state plus permitted dramatic content; `CampaignContract` and `IntentContract` define scope, authority, and preconditions. A recognition card should link back to the exact `StateTx`, permit, manifest, or evidence object used.

## Contradiction quarantine: aviation, e-discovery, and wiki mechanisms

The FAA’s Safety Management System separates **hazard identification and risk control** (Safety Risk Management) from **continued effectiveness checks** (Safety Assurance), supported by employee reporting, audits, data analysis, documented processes, accountability, and lessons learned [4](https://www.faa.gov/about/initiatives/sms/explained/components). This is a direct pattern for a contradiction lane: accept a player report as a high-priority hazard signal, freeze the disputed field from automatic mutation, assess competing claims, apply a controlled resolution, and later audit whether the control worked. A contradiction should be non-punitive and easy to report; reporting must not silently rewrite canon.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26 provides a useful e-discovery analogy: withheld material must be expressly identified and described sufficiently to assess the claim; information subject to a resolved protection claim may need to be returned, sequestered, or destroyed, while the producing party preserves it until resolution [5](https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_26). In SynapticGM, quarantine should preserve both claims and provenance while preventing disputed evidence from driving gameplay. Suggested object:

```json
{
  "contradictionId": "cx-184",
  "field": "npc.mira.coins",
  "claims": [{"value": 3, "source": "StateTx-184"}, {"value": 0, "source": "player-correction-22"}],
  "status": "quarantined",
  "authorityOrder": ["player-correction", "pinned-canon", "accepted-StateTx"],
  "blockedMutations": true,
  "preserveOriginals": true,
  "resolution": null
}
```

The MediaWiki model supplies concrete recognition and rollback affordances: page history retains revisions; users compare any two revisions, link to an exact historical version, and revert to an earlier version [6](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Help:History). Apply this to state: immutable append-only transactions, side-by-side diff of competing claims, a stable permalink to each version, and an explicit compensating transaction rather than destructive edit. A “current manifest” must be reproducible from the ledger at a named revision, not from a mutable summary.

## Concrete acceptance gates and endurance tests

1. **Authority gate:** reject any mutation to protected fields unless the request is an accepted `StateTx` satisfying the current `CampaignContract`; prose, RAG snippets, summaries, and `SceneManifest` alone cannot mutate state.
2. **Introduction gate:** a new named entity requires a valid `IntroductionPermit`; it must declare identity, first-seen turn, permitted scene scope, and whether it is canon, evidence, or draft.
3. **Conflict gate:** if two non-compatible values target the same entity/version, create `ContradictionRecord`, preserve both claims, quarantine the field, and route resolution to player correction or an explicit adjudication action.
4. **Recognition gate:** every durable correction returns transaction ID, before/after diff, authority reason, and affected projections; the next scene must visibly acknowledge the corrected value when relevant.
5. **Beat gate:** `beatFingerprint` detects repeated or already-resolved beats but cannot override ledger truth; a blocked duplicate should produce a new permitted beat or a transparent “already resolved” acknowledgment.
6. **Endurance suite:** replay deterministic 100/250/500-turn scenarios with compaction, retrieval misses, stale evidence, tool failures, contradictory NPC testimony, and player corrections. Measure invariant violations, unauthorized mutations, correction persistence, quarantine leakage, duplicate-hook rate, false-completion rate, and recovery latency. Require zero unauthorized protected-field mutations, zero quarantine leakage into committed state, and 100% reproducible replay for committed transactions.

## References

[1] Xinyu Jessica Wang et al., “The Long-Horizon Task Mirage? Diagnosing Where and Why Agentic Systems Break” | https://arxiv.org/html/2604.11978v1  
[2] Brennan Jones et al., “Users’ Expectations and Practices with Agent Memory” | https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3706599.3720158  
[3] ArticuLab, “Conversational Grounding” | https://www.justinecassell.com/articulab/projects/convers-ground/  
[4] Federal Aviation Administration, “Safety Management System: Components” | https://www.faa.gov/about/initiatives/sms/explained/components  
[5] Legal Information Institute, “Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 26” | https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_26  
[6] MediaWiki, “Help:History” | https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Help:History

results.input: Ledger-first long-memory architecture: event sourcing, CQRS, accounting, OS paging, Git history, EHR and case management; working-set prompt assembly; multi-session rehydration; IDs/aliases; provenance; append-only snapshots and hashes.

output.confidence_notes: The evidence is strong for the core architectural patterns: Fowler’s event-sourcing and CQRS essays are influential but explicitly dated/draft-style guidance rather than normative standards; Kafka’s durability, ordering, retention, replication, and exactly-once language is product documentation whose guarantees depend on deployment and API configuration; Git reflogs are local, expirable recovery metadata and must not be treated as a permanent append-only ledger. W3C PROV-DM is a 2013 Recommendation, while the cited HL7 FHIR R5 Provenance and AuditEvent pages are current published R5 Trial-Use specifications, not legal or compliance advice. The OS working-set analogy and the proposed SynapticGM schemas/tests are engineering extrapolations, not claims that the cited sources prescribe this game architecture. Any security, retention, or evidentiary policy should be reviewed by qualified counsel and validated against the actual storage, threat model, and jurisdiction.

# Research Notes

## Ledger-first pattern and authority boundary

Event sourcing stores each domain change as an ordered event sequence, allowing state reconstruction, temporal queries, replay, and rebuilds; snapshots are derived accelerators rather than substitutes for the event log.[1] CQRS separates the command model from read models, but Fowler cautions that it adds substantial complexity and should be limited to domains where the benefit is clear.[2] For SynapticGM, therefore, **StateTx is the only authoritative mutable-world write**: a validated, append-only transaction with stream sequence, actor, causal parent, schema version, and idempotency key. A `SceneManifest` is a replayable/materialized read projection. RAG text, summaries, and prompt prose remain supporting evidence or draft invention and cannot promote themselves into inventory, quest, roster, HP, or other world truth.

Kafka’s official documentation provides a useful distributed-log comparison: events have keys, values, timestamps, and headers; keyed events in a partition preserve write order; topics retain events for later and retrospective processing and can be replicated.[3] A solo-founder implementation need not adopt Kafka, but should borrow the invariants: per-campaign or per-aggregate ordering, durable append, replay from a sequence, explicit retention policy, and a separate projection checkpoint. Any claim of “exactly once” is **SPECULATIVE unless demonstrated for the selected storage and side-effect path**; use idempotency and an outbox for external effects.

## Mechanism mapping to SynapticGM

| Established mechanism | SynapticGM mapping | Concrete implementation gate |
|---|---|---|
| Event-sourced command/write model [1] | `StateTx` | Append only after invariant, authorization, and optimistic-concurrency checks; reject mutation without expected prior sequence. |
| CQRS read projection [2] | `SceneManifest` | Rebuildable from StateTx; store `projectionVersion`, `lastAppliedSeq`, and deterministic projection hash. |
| Command contracts and bounded-context decisions [2] | `IntentContract`, `IntroductionPermit`, `CampaignContract` | Treat as preconditions/authorization artifacts; no contract may directly mutate state. |
| Derived stream/query view [1][2] | `HookArc` | Mark as projection with source sequence range; regenerate after replay or contract revision. |
| Content-addressed history and named refs (Git analogy) [4] | Stable opaque IDs, aliases, campaign refs, and snapshot pointers | Store immutable object/hash plus mutable alias/ref separately; resolve aliases at read time and record the resolved ID in the transaction. |
| Provenance entity/activity/agent/derivation model [5] | StateTx, evidence, generator/tool, player correction, and SceneManifest derivation edges | Every derived claim records target version, source IDs, activity, actor/agent, timestamp, and confidence/status. |
| Deterministic content fingerprint | `beatFingerprint` | Hash normalized beat inputs plus contract/canon version; use as dedupe key and regression-test fixture, never as authority. |

## Working-set assembly and multi-session rehydration

The operating-systems “working set” analogy is useful only as a **budgeting pattern**: assemble a bounded prompt from the current authoritative state plus the smallest causally relevant recent history, pinned canon/opening invariant, active contracts, and selected evidence. Page in older ledger segments or summaries when needed, but summaries are cache/index material. A prompt assembler should return both the text and a manifest of included StateTx sequence ranges, IDs, aliases resolved, source versions, token estimate, and omission reasons. If an authoritative transaction or required reference is missing, it should fail closed or ask for reconciliation rather than fill the gap with semantic retrieval.

A session rehydrates by loading a verified snapshot, checking its campaign/aggregate ID, schema version, last sequence, and hash, then replaying StateTx after that sequence. The replay must be deterministic: the same snapshot plus event suffix must yield the same state hash and SceneManifest. Snapshot creation may occur concurrently with normal operation, but the snapshot records the exact sequence boundary; a torn or hash-mismatched snapshot is quarantined and rebuilt from the ledger.[1]

## IDs, aliases, provenance, and append-only integrity

Use globally unique opaque IDs for entities and transactions; human names are aliases, not identity. An alias table should be append-only or versioned with effective intervals, collision checks, and explicit rename events. Git’s reflog demonstrates the value of recording where a mutable reference pointed over time, but the official documentation also states that reflogs are pruned by expiration and are therefore a recovery aid, not a permanent audit ledger.[4]

W3C PROV-DM defines provenance around entities, activities, agents, derivations, bundles, and identifiers, expressly to support assessments of quality, reliability, and trustworthiness.[5] HL7 FHIR’s Provenance resource adds an implementation-relevant rule: references to resources, entities, and agents must be unique and unambiguous, and version information is needed when versions matter.[6] Its AuditEvent resource separates event-time audit records from record-keeping provenance and notes that duplicate actor records can help detect problems; audit stores generally should not accept update/delete operations because that compromises integrity.[7] Applied here, preserve both: a StateTx’s immutable provenance assertion (“how this fact came to be”) and operational audit (“who read, proposed, accepted, rejected, or replayed it”).

A practical snapshot envelope is: `snapshotId`, `campaignId`, `aggregateId`, `lastAppliedSeq`, `stateSchemaVersion`, `projectionVersion`, canonical serialization, `stateHash`, `parentSnapshotHash`, creation activity/agent, and source ledger range. Hashes detect corruption and accidental divergence; they do not prove that an event was truthful at creation. For stronger tamper evidence, chain each StateTx with `prevTxHash` and hash the canonical envelope, while separately protecting keys and backups.

## Failure modes and tests

| Failure mode | Required gate or test |
|---|---|
| Two writers accept the same prior state | Compare `expectedSeq` atomically; integration test concurrent append conflict. |
| Duplicate delivery or retry | Unique `(campaignId, txId)` and idempotency key; replay duplicate twice and assert one state change. |
| Projection drift | Rebuild SceneManifest from genesis and from snapshots; hashes must match. |
| Stale or colliding alias | Alias resolution test across rename intervals; reject ambiguous names and persist resolved opaque ID. |
| Snapshot corruption/torn write | Verify canonical hash and parent hash; quarantine mismatch and replay from prior valid snapshot. |
| Replay repeats external side effects | Outbox with transaction-bound effect IDs; replay mode suppresses or deduplicates sends. |
| Prompt hallucination promoted to fact | Schema test: only accepted StateTx can change authoritative fields; every prompt fact carries source sequence or is labeled evidence/draft. |
| Contract/permit bypass | Property tests that invalid `IntentContract`, missing `IntroductionPermit`, or expired `CampaignContract` cannot append StateTx. |
| Non-deterministic generation | Fixed seed/input fixtures for `beatFingerprint`; compare normalized output and state hash across replays. |

### References

[1]: https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/EventSourcing.html "Martin Fowler, Event Sourcing"
[2]: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html "Martin Fowler, CQRS"
[3]: https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/ "Apache Kafka Documentation"
[4]: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog "Git git-reflog Documentation"
[5]: https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/ "W3C PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model"
[6]: https://www.hl7.org/fhir/provenance.html "HL7 FHIR R5 Provenance"
[7]: https://www.hl7.org/fhir/auditevent.html "HL7 FHIR R5 AuditEvent"

output.confidence_notes: The technical mechanisms are supported by primary papers or official project documentation, but benchmark results are dated research measurements and do not establish production correctness for SynapticGM. The Letta README confirms current local/self-hosted positioning while explicitly marking the retired V1 server unsupported; version-specific behavior must therefore be revalidated before adoption. Exact API rates and cloud GPU prices are time- and region-sensitive; the break-even equations are decision scaffolding, not a forecast. No universal indie self-host/API crossover was found in authoritative sources, so any numeric utilization or cost claim beyond measured workload data should be marked **SPECULATIVE**. GraphRAG, RAG, recurrent memory, summaries, adapters, and draft models are treated here only as supporting/proposal mechanisms; counsel should review model/data licenses, privacy, retention, and third-party service terms before production use.
output.research_notes:
# Research Notes

## Reality check: use model memory as a proposal layer, not a ledger

The strongest implementation pattern is **ledger-first orchestration with model memory behind a typed boundary**. Long-context, recurrent/compressive memory, RAG/GraphRAG, fine-tuning, and agent-memory frameworks can improve recall, style, planning, and evidence selection, but none should be allowed to authoritatively mutate inventory, quests, roster, HP, relationship values, or other world truth. A model may emit a proposed `StateTx`; a deterministic validator checks the current ledger, `CampaignContract`, `IntentContract`, permissions, preconditions, and idempotency before commit. The committed transaction is then rendered into a `SceneManifest`.

### Mechanism comparison and SynapticGM mapping

| Mechanism | What the evidence supports | Safe SynapticGM use | Required gate/test |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Long context** | More tokens provide access to more recent/prompted material, but attention cost and KV-cache memory grow with context; long-context capability is not equivalent to reliable state tracking. Infini-attention instead combines local attention with a bounded associative compressive memory and reports 1M-token passkey and 500K-token summarization experiments, but this is a model/training research result, not a production correctness guarantee [1]. | Put immutable opening invariant and a compact, read-only ledger snapshot in context. Use for scene coherence and `HookArc`/`beatFingerprint` continuity, never as authority. | Context assembler must include ledger revision/hash and only current authoritative projections. Test contradiction prompts, stale snapshots, and long-session recall; reject any proposed mutation whose precondition or revision does not match. |
| **Recurrent/compressive memory** | Infini-attention updates a learned associative matrix from KV states and retrieves with queries; this is lossy learned memory, unlike an append-only event log [1]. Transformer-XL-style recurrence and similar approaches preserve selected prior context, not exact transactional history. | Treat recurrent memory as a cache for supporting evidence, character voice, unresolved motifs, or candidate `HookArc`s. Store pointers to StateTx IDs, not canonical facts. | Memory entries require provenance, source StateTx IDs, timestamp, confidence, and scope. A replay test must prove that deleting/rebuilding learned memory leaves ledger-derived world state unchanged. |
| **RAG / GraphRAG** | Microsoft’s GraphRAG builds a graph plus hierarchical community summaries to improve discovery over private corpora; it is a retrieval/context method, not a transaction system [2]. RAG can expose relevant evidence, but retrieved text may be stale, incomplete, or adversarial. | Use GraphRAG to retrieve prior scenes, evidence excerpts, canon notes, and candidate causal links supporting `IntroductionPermit`, `CampaignContract`, `HookArc`, or beat planning. The result may explain a proposal but cannot override a StateTx. | Every retrieved item carries document/scene/transaction ID, revision, provenance, and retrieval timestamp. Require exact ledger lookup for any claim about mutable world state. Add tests for stale retrieval, conflicting documents, prompt injection, and “summary says X / ledger says not-X.” |
| **LoRA / QLoRA** | QLoRA freezes a 4-bit quantized base model and trains low-rank adapters; the paper reports fitting a 65B model on one 48GB GPU while preserving task performance in its benchmark, with NF4, double quantization, and paged optimizers [3]. This demonstrates adaptation efficiency, not guaranteed safety or truth preservation. | Train adapters for output schema discipline, narrative tone, scene formatting, tool-call conventions, and classification of intent. Keep canon and mutable state external. A versioned adapter may be selected by `CampaignContract` or scene mode. | Adapter registry includes base-model hash, dataset hash, rank/quantization settings, evaluation set, license, and rollback ID. Run schema-validity, refusal, contradiction, and StateTx precondition tests before promotion. Never fine-tune on unreviewed ledger mutations as if they were truth. |
| **Distillation / small-model routing** | Distillation can reduce serving cost/latency, but quality depends on teacher coverage and the target task; a small model should not silently replace a stronger model on high-risk state operations. | Route low-risk tasks—beat labeling, `beatFingerprint` extraction, evidence ranking, format repair, and draft dialogue—to a local/small model. Route ambiguous intent, multi-constraint planning, and transaction proposals to a stronger model. | `IntentContract` declares task class, risk, budget, and required model tier. Shadow-evaluate routed versus reference outputs; enforce escalation on uncertainty, low validator score, novel entities, or failed structured output. |
| **Speculative decoding** | vLLM documents model-based and simpler speculative methods and states they target inter-token latency, especially medium-to-low-QPS, memory-bound workloads; speedups are workload-dependent rather than guaranteed [4]. | Use a small draft model to accelerate generation of narration or tool-call candidates. Keep the target model/verifier and deterministic transaction validator authoritative. | Measure acceptance rate, p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, and cost by route. Disable speculation when acceptance falls below threshold or when structured output/tool-call correctness regresses. Do not treat draft output as an accepted StateTx. |
| **Local open-weight inference** | Letta’s current project supports local/self-hosted agents and identifies itself as the successor to MemGPT; its README also warns that the retired V1 server is unsupported [5]. Open-weight deployment is technically feasible, but GPU, RAM, electricity, operations, model updates, and concurrency are real costs. | A local model can handle offline drafting, privacy-sensitive evidence work, deterministic format repair, and low-risk `SceneManifest` prose. Letta-like memory blocks can map to working-memory caches, while the SynapticGM ledger remains separate. | Pin model/container/driver versions; health-check context length, quantization, structured-output support, and throughput. Add failover to API or another local model. Treat vendor/framework claims as implementation guidance, not correctness evidence. |

## Contract-level design

`IntentContract` should be the ingress envelope: task type, player/session ID, campaign ID, ledger revision, permitted tools, risk tier, latency/cost budget, and required output schema. `IntroductionPermit` should be checked before a model may propose introducing a person, faction, item, or location; the permit should reference the opening invariant, canon pins, and existing roster. `CampaignContract` should select allowed model/adapters, context policy, retrieval namespaces, and escalation rules. `HookArc` and `beatFingerprint` are useful as planning/state-adjacent structures: the model may suggest a hook or beat fingerprint, but acceptance requires compatibility with the committed ledger and campaign constraints.

A `StateTx` proposal should contain transaction ID, base ledger revision, actor/tool identity, typed operations, exact preconditions, evidence references, and a deterministic validation result. The commit path should be: **proposal → schema validation → authorization/permit checks → ledger precondition check → invariant/property tests → append/commit → projection → SceneManifest**. The model must not receive a tool that directly writes canonical state. A `SceneManifest` should include the committed transaction IDs and ledger revision used to render it, so replay and audit can distinguish accepted world changes from draft invention.

## Self-host versus API break-even

Do not assert a universal break-even price. Compute it from measured workload:

`monthly_API_cost = input_tokens × input_rate + output_tokens × output_rate + cached/storage/tool charges`.

`monthly_self_host_cost = amortized_hardware + electricity + storage/network + maintenance + operator time + standby utilization penalty`.

Break-even utilization is approximately `fixed_monthly_self_host_cost / (API_cost_per_request − variable_self_host_cost_per_request)`. For a solo-founder narrative game, API-first is usually the lower-risk default during low or uncertain traffic because it avoids idle GPU capacity and operations. A local model becomes attractive when privacy/offline requirements, sustained high utilization, predictable workloads, or a capable existing GPU dominate. Use measured tokens/request, concurrency, latency, and quality—not headline model size—to choose.

A practical staged route is: API reference model for benchmark and difficult planning; local open-weight model for low-risk drafting and extraction; optional QLoRA adapter after a stable, versioned dataset; speculative decoding only after route-level latency measurements. Keep a per-request ledger of model, adapter, prompt/context hash, retrieved evidence IDs, token counts, validator outcomes, retries, and escalation reason. This enables an actual break-even decision rather than a vendor estimate.

## Failure modes and concrete tests

The main failures are **memory hallucination**, stale or conflicting retrieval, learned-memory overwrite, adapter-induced schema drift, quantization quality loss, speculative-decoding regressions, unsupported local-server updates, and cost models that ignore idle time. Required tests include ledger replay after deleting all RAG and learned-memory indexes; conflict tests where a summary contradicts a StateTx; duplicate transaction and retry/idempotency tests; introduction of an unpermitted entity; stale revision/concurrent-write tests; adversarial retrieved text containing instructions; structured-output fuzzing; adapter rollback; quantized-versus-reference evaluation; and route escalation under uncertainty. Pass criteria should be expressed as invariants—for example, no committed `StateTx` without valid preconditions, and no `SceneManifest` claiming a mutable fact absent from its cited ledger revision.

### References

[1]: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.07143v1
[2]: https://microsoft.github.io/graphrag/
[3]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14314
[4]: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/speculative_decoding/
[5]: https://github.com/cpacker/MemGPT/blob/main/README.md

results.input: Text inference vendor and routing economics: official pricing and capabilities for direct APIs and open-weight hosts; batch/flex/prompt caching; commercial reliability/ToS and EU/UK residency; a Free/Mid/High ladder with cautious current-date caveats.

output.confidence_notes: Pricing, model names, introductory offers, supported features, regions, quotas, and endpoint availability are volatile and must be rechecked at implementation time; all rates and capabilities above are date-stamped to 2026-08-18 and should be stored with the router’s price-sheet revision. Vendor pages are authoritative for advertised terms, not independent proof of uptime, quality, or EU/UK residency. The Together 99% SLA statement is a vendor announcement and is **SPECULATIVE for production reliance until confirmed in executed terms**; similarly, any free-tier, promotional-credit, or community-host claim is **SPECULATIVE** unless verified in the active account and contract. This is implementation research, not legal advice: counsel should review DPA/SCC/UK transfer, retention, subprocessors, acceptable-use, termination, model-deprecation, and regional-processing terms before routing player data.
output.research_notes:
# Research Notes

## Actionable vendor/routing comparison (confirmed at 2026-08-18)

| Route | Confirmed economics/capability | SynapticGM use and gate |
|---|---|---|
| **Premium direct API (High)** | OpenAI’s current pricing page presents flagship/balanced/low-cost model classes and documents **Batch at 50% off**, cached-input rates, **Flex** lower-cost processing with slower responses and possible unavailability, and enterprise options such as SLAs and regional processing [1]. Anthropic’s Messages Batches API charges **50% of standard input/output rates**, supports active models and most Messages features, and usually completes in under one hour but can expire at 24 hours [4]. | Use High for `IntentContract` adjudication, `IntroductionPermit` checks, and final `StateTx` proposal generation only when latency, reasoning, or ambiguity warrants it. A vendor response is never authority: accept only after schema validation, canon/player-correction precedence, deterministic conflict checks, and ledger append transaction. |
| **Mid route (balanced direct or hosted open-weight)** | Anthropic documents model families by capability and supports tool use, structured requests, extended thinking, and batching [3][4]. Google’s official Agent Platform/Vertex pricing page is the authoritative place to check model- and region-specific rates and currently advertises introductory Gemini rates through Dec. 31, 2026 [7]. Together and Fireworks expose serverless open-weight inference; Fireworks explicitly documents per-token pricing and 50%-priced batch inference [8]. | Use Mid for ordinary scene drafting, `SceneManifest` candidates, HookArc/beatFingerprint extraction, and evidence classification. Require output JSON with `state_tx_candidates[]`, `scene_manifest`, `evidence_refs[]`, `authority_level`, and `uncertainties[]`; reject any candidate that mutates inventory/HP/roster without a corresponding validated transaction. |
| **Free/Low route** | Low-cost small models and open-weight serverless endpoints are economically attractive, but public price/model availability changes frequently. Together’s official pricing page states serverless, dedicated endpoints, fine-tuning, and GPU-cluster options [9]; its model documentation lists per-token serverless rates [10]. Treat any “free tier,” promotional credit, or community endpoint as **SPECULATIVE until verified in the account and current price sheet**. | Use Low for beat classification, deduplication, style suggestions, cacheable evidence summaries, and non-authoritative draft invention. Never allow Low output to directly commit `StateTx`, resolve canon conflicts, or grant an `IntroductionPermit`. |

## Cost controls and prompt layout

Prompt caching is useful when the request repeats a stable prefix: system policy, schema, canon snapshot, and tool definitions should precede variable player input. OpenAI states that caching is automatic for eligible recent models, requires exact prefix matches, exposes `cached_tokens`, and supports explicit breakpoints/keys; the current documentation says eligible prompts generally start at 1,024 tokens and later-model cache writes can have their own charge [2]. Anthropic supports automatic or explicit `cache_control`, with documented 5-minute default and optional 1-hour lifetime at additional cost [3].

For SynapticGM, place the immutable product law, `CampaignContract` version, canonical opening invariant, StateTx schema, and stable `beatFingerprint` rubric in a versioned cache prefix. Append the current accepted-ledger projection, player correction, and scene-specific request after the breakpoint. Never cache mutable world truth in a way that can outlive a ledger revision: include `ledger_revision` and `canon_version` in the cache key, and invalidate on correction or transaction commit. Record `cache_hit`, cached-token count, prompt version, and vendor/model in the cost/audit event.

Batch is appropriate for offline evaluation, regression tests, beat fingerprinting, evidence labeling, and nightly draft generation. It is **not** suitable for an interactive turn requiring an immediate `StateTx`; model results should be staged as proposals and revalidated when applied. OpenAI documents a 24-hour batch completion window [1], and Anthropic documents up to 100,000 requests/256 MB per batch, typical completion under one hour, 24-hour expiry, and 29-day result availability [4]. Add `batch_job_id`, request IDs, deadline, retry count, and `source_ledger_revision` to every staged artifact.

Flex/low-priority processing is an economic route rather than a correctness route. OpenAI explicitly warns of slower responses and occasional 429 resource-unavailable errors, recommends exponential backoff, and suggests retrying on standard processing when success is worth the extra cost [5]. Gate Flex to non-interactive work; for an interactive turn, use a deadline-aware fallback to standard Mid/High, never silently convert a failed proposal into a committed transaction.

## Commercial reliability, terms, and residency gates

Do not infer reliability from marketing latency claims. Require an operational contract or published SLA before promising availability. OpenAI’s pricing FAQ says enterprise customers may receive SLAs, lower latency, and related commitments through enterprise offerings [1]. Together reports provisioned throughput with a 99% uptime SLA in a July 2026 announcement, but that is a vendor announcement and must be checked against the signed service terms before relying on it [11]. Fireworks describes high rate limits and postpaid billing on its pricing page, while its current capacity and model availability remain vendor-controlled [8].

For personal data or sensitive player content, route by residency policy before model selection. OpenAI links regional processing/data residency to enterprise offerings and notes a data-residency price modifier on its pricing page [1]. Anthropic’s commercial DPA incorporates SCCs into its Commercial Terms [6], but an SCC/DPA is a transfer mechanism, **not proof that all processing or support occurs in the EU/UK**. Require a vendor-specific region, retention, subprocessor, and transfer assessment; if the requirement is strict EU/UK residency, prefer a contractually documented regional deployment or self-hosted/open-weight inference, and block unverified routes.

## Concrete validation and failure tests

The router should select `(vendor, model, service_tier, region, cache_policy)` from an allow-listed capability matrix, then emit a `RouteDecision` containing price-sheet revision, residency class, timeout, retry budget, and authority ceiling. Contract tests should verify that every model path returns schema-valid JSON; malformed JSON, missing `authority_level`, stale `ledger_revision`, unsupported tools, or region mismatch becomes a rejected proposal. Replay tests should submit identical `(ledger_revision, player_correction, IntentContract)` inputs and require deterministic transaction validation even if prose differs. Chaos tests should inject 429/5xx/timeouts, cache misses, batch expiry, model deprecation, and provider disagreement; the expected behavior is retry/fallback or human-visible draft, never an implicit world-state mutation.

The central economic rule is **route for cost and latency, but authorize by the ledger**. RAG, summaries, cached context, and model “memory” can support flavor/evidence only; `StateTx` remains the sole world-truth write path under player correction > pinned canon/opening invariant > accepted transaction > SceneManifest > evidence > draft invention.

## References

[2]: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching “OpenAI Prompt Caching”
[3]: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching “Anthropic Prompt Caching”
[4]: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing “Anthropic Batch Processing”
[5]: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/flex-processing “OpenAI Flex Processing”
[6]: https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996862-how-do-i-view-and-sign-your-data-processing-addendum-dpa “Anthropic DPA”
[7]: https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/generative-ai/pricing “Google Agent Platform Generative AI Pricing”
[8]: https://docs.fireworks.ai/serverless/pricing “Fireworks Serverless Pricing”

[10]: https://docs.together.ai/docs/serverless/models “Together AI Serverless Models”

# Research Notes

## 1. Cost and deployment alternatives

**Recommended architecture:** treat splash art as a non-authoritative, cacheable presentation artifact. A request may be proposed by an `IntentContract`, but only a validated `StateTx` can establish world truth. The resulting `SceneManifest` should carry an optional `artRef` plus generation provenance; it must never be used to infer inventory, quests, roster, HP, identity, or other state.

| Route | Confirmed mechanism/cost evidence | Controllability, filtering, and operational fit |
|---|---|---|
| **BFL direct / FLUX** | BFL documents credit pricing at **$0.01/credit**. As of access date, FLUX.2 Klein starts at **$0.014/image** for 4B and **$0.015/image** for 9B; Pro starts at **$0.03/image**, Max at **$0.07**, Flex at **$0.05**; pricing scales with output megapixels. FLUX.2 Dev is local-only and non-commercial under the cited documentation. FLUX.1 Pro is listed at $0.04/image. [1] | Direct access gives a narrow vendor surface and predictable per-output budgeting. BFL lists Flex for fine-grained control/typography and provides open-weight licensing tiers, but exact commercial rights and model-specific safety behavior must be checked against the applicable license before shipping. Use a pinned model/version, seed, dimensions, prompt hash, and policy result in `SceneManifest`. |
| **Replicate** | Replicate says usage is pay-as-you-go: models may bill by hardware time or input/output, and model pages provide estimates. Its pricing page currently shows examples including FLUX 1.1 Pro at **$0.04/output image**, FLUX Dev at **$0.09/output image**, and FLUX Schnell at **$0.025/output image**. [2] | Broad model choice and easy fallback, but the abstraction can change model availability and price. Pin an owner/model/version digest; reject unpinned aliases. Treat vendor safety/filtering as a defense-in-depth check, not as a canon validator. |
| **fal Model APIs** | fal documents prepaid credits, per-model units, and billing only for successful outputs. Images are generally billed per image or megapixel; server errors and queue waiting are not charged. fal exposes a pricing API, with an example endpoint returning unit price and unit. [3] | Strong fit for a cost-aware gateway: query price before generation, reserve a weekly budget, and record actual billed units. The “successful output only” rule supports retry policy, but application-level timeouts and duplicate submissions still require idempotency keys. |
| **ComfyUI/local** | The official repository describes a modular node-graph engine with reusable workflows, local API, asynchronous queueing, partial graph re-execution, offline execution, seeds/workflow recovery, masks, ControlNets, reference conditioning, and support for SDXL, SD3.5, Flux and other models. [4] | Best for repeatability, privacy, deterministic test fixtures, and avoiding per-image vendor charges once hardware is available. It does not make compute free: measure GPU time, power, storage, model downloads, maintenance, and queue occupancy. Pin workflow JSON, checkpoint hash, LoRA/control assets, sampler, seed, and ComfyUI commit. Custom nodes are a supply-chain risk; allow-list and hash them. |
| **SDXL / SD3-family / AuraFlow** | SDXL is available as an open model card; Stability’s current image-model page describes self-hosted Stable Diffusion 3.5 and API options, while fal presents AuraFlow v0.3 as an open-source flow-based model with commercial use supported on its model page. [5] [6] | These are alternatives, not interchangeable assets. License, safety, output quality, typography, conditioning, VRAM, and hosted price vary by exact checkpoint and date. Do not state that “open” means unrestricted commercial use; attach a license identifier and approval status to the generation request. **Any unverified claim about relative quality, censorship/filter bypass, or price superiority is SPECULATIVE.** |

### Soft-skip and weekly cap policy

Use a two-stage gate. First, `IntroductionPermit`/`CampaignContract` decides whether the scene is eligible for memorable art: canon/opening invariant and accepted `StateTx` must already exist; the request must be attached to a valid `HookArc` and stable `beatFingerprint`; and the scene must not be a routine turn. Second, a cost/policy gate decides whether to render. If budget, safety, continuity, or provider health fails, **soft-skip** to a text-only or previously cached `SceneManifest`; never block state progression and never invent a replacement fact.

A practical solo-founder default is a weekly dollar cap plus an image-count cap, with lower caps for exploratory drafts and a small reserved pool for player-correction or canon-critical presentation. Exact numbers are product policy, not source facts. Enforce an atomic reservation ledger keyed by `(campaignId, week, requestFingerprint)`, an idempotency key, and a maximum retry count. Record `estimatedCost`, `reservedCost`, `actualCost`, `currency`, `provider`, `modelVersion`, `outputMP`, `safetyDecision`, and `skipReason`. A cache hit should cost zero provider calls and must remain tied to the same `beatFingerprint` and approved visual intent.

## 2. Continuity and non-game truth patterns

The useful cross-domain pattern is **append-only evidence plus explicit correction/reversal**, not “the latest summary wins.” NIST defines provenance as the chronology of origin, development, ownership, location, and changes to data/system components. [7] FDA guidance, while specific to drug CGMP and nonbinding outside that domain, says data should be reliable and accurate, backups exact and complete, records protected from alteration/loss, and audit trails reviewed according to risk. [8] Git’s official `revert` mechanism records a new commit reversing an earlier commit rather than deleting the original history. [9]

Map these patterns as follows:

* `StateTx` is the append-only accepted transaction, with actor, timestamp/sequence, causal parent, schema version, precondition result, and hash. A correction is a new compensating `StateTx`, not mutation of history.
* `SceneManifest` is a derived, reproducible projection: it contains the accepted ledger head, manifest hash, evidence refs, and optional art provenance. Regenerate it after correction; do not let prose or an image update the ledger.
* `IntentContract` is a request/authorization envelope, analogous to a controlled work order: requested effect, scope, player-visible purpose, budget class, safety policy, and expiry. It is not an event.
* `IntroductionPermit` is an admission gate for introducing a character/object/faction. It should require a canonical identity or an explicitly marked draft invention, plus conflict checks against pinned canon and current ledger.
* `CampaignContract` is the durable policy/configuration boundary: allowed providers, licenses, weekly cap, retention, filter policy, and rollback semantics.
* `HookArc` and `beatFingerprint` are continuity keys for presentation and pacing. They may justify a splash-art opportunity and deduplicate retries, but they are not evidence of a world event.

A minimal provenance object should include: `sourceType` (`playerCorrection|canon|stateTx|manifest|evidence|draft`), `sourceId`, `parentHash`, `createdAt`, `author`, `schemaVersion`, `contentHash`, `supersedes`/`compensates`, and `reviewStatus`. A manifest test should fail closed if an image prompt contradicts accepted state, references an unpermitted identity, or lacks a ledger-head hash. A replay test should rebuild the same manifest from the same ledger and pinned inputs. A correction test should prove that old manifests remain inspectable but new manifests reflect the compensating transaction. A cost test should prove duplicate request fingerprints cannot double-reserve budget.

## 3. Failure modes and concrete gates

**Failure mode: image becomes accidental authority.** Gate: renderer receives a read-only `SceneManifest` projection, never raw model output as state input; generated captions/OCR are quarantined as supporting evidence.

**Failure mode: provider/model drift.** Gate: require immutable model/version identifiers, workflow/checkpoint hashes, and a compatibility test before promotion; aliases are rejected in production.

**Failure mode: filter mismatch or unsafe output.** Gate: preflight prompt policy, provider moderation where available, post-generation classifier/human review for memorable art, and a quarantine state. A filter pass is not canon approval.

**Failure mode: retries exceed cap or duplicate charge.** Gate: atomic budget reservation, idempotency key, provider request ID, bounded retry, and reconciliation against provider usage. fal’s documented successful-output billing helps but does not replace these controls. [3]

**Failure mode: continuity drift.** Gate: compare the proposed visual intent against pinned canon, accepted `StateTx`, and current roster/asset constraints; if uncertain, soft-skip rather than “repair” truth through generation.

**Failure mode: mutable correction erases history.** Gate: append compensating transactions and preserve superseded manifests, following the audit/provenance and Git-revert pattern. [7] [8] [9]

## References

[1]: https://docs.bfl.ml/quick_start/pricing "Black Forest Labs FLUX pricing documentation"
[2]: https://replicate.com/pricing "Replicate pricing"
[3]: https://fal.ai/docs/documentation/model-apis/pricing "fal Model API pricing"
[4]: https://github.com/comfy-org/ComfyUI "ComfyUI official repository"
[5]: https://stability.ai/stable-image "Stability AI image models"
[6]: https://fal.ai/models/fal-ai/aura-flow "fal AuraFlow v0.3 model page"
[7]: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5.pdf "NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5"
[8]: https://www.fda.gov/media/119267/download "FDA Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP Guidance"
[9]: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert "Git revert documentation"
